raw_response:
I've been farming these 7 mu in Quzhou for 40 years now. My father farmed them before me. I'm 60 this year, and my back isn't what it used to be, but I still know every inch of this land. I finished middle school — back then that was something — so I can read the fertilizer bags and understand what the extension agent says, but honestly, I trust my own eyes more than anyone's numbers.

My household has seven people. My oldest son and his wife work at a factory in Handan, so they're only back for planting and harvest. My wife, my daughter-in-law, and me do most of the daily work. My grandson is in school. We get by because my son sends money back, but I don't like relying on that. The farm has to pay for itself.

This year, like last year, I'll plant wheat on 4 mu after the maize comes off. The east field does well with wheat — it's the better soil. I'll plant around October 12th, same as my neighbors. I save my own wheat seed most years, but I bought fresh Jinmai seed two years ago and the yield was good, so I'll use what I saved from that. I'll put down about 50 jin of compound fertilizer per mu at planting — that's my base. Then at jointing, if the wheat looks a bit yellow, I'll topdress with urea, maybe another 20 jin per mu. Total nitrogen comes to about 16-17 kg per mu. I irrigate three times: once after planting if it's dry, once at jointing, and once at heading. The well water isn't free anymore — they meter it now — so I watch that carefully. I expect about 450 kg per mu if the winter isn't too dry.

Maize goes in the same 4 mu right after wheat harvest, around June 15th. That's always a rush. Sometimes I hire the combine for wheat and we plant maize the same day. I buy hybrid maize seed every year — can't save hybrid seed. That's 50 yuan per mu, but it's worth it. For fertilizer, I do base compound at planting and topdress urea at the 6-leaf stage, about 15 kg N total per mu. Two irrigations usually — one at jointing and one at filling. Last year I got 500 kg/mu, but I'll say 480 this year to be safe. Prices have been up and down.

The west 2 mu I'll keep in cotton. My wife is good at picking, and cotton gives us cash in the fall when we need it for school fees and winter clothes. I plant in late April. Cotton needs less fertilizer than grain — maybe 12 kg N per mu, split between base and flowering. But it needs more pesticide. The bollworms come some years and not others. I spray insecticide two or three times and use herbicide once. Two irrigations, usually. Picking is all family labor — my wife and daughter-in-law do most of it, four or five rounds from September to October. I expect about 220 kg of lint per mu if the weather cooperates.

The remaining 1 mu I'll plant watermelon. It's risky, but last year I made good money at the county market. I plant in late April under plastic mulch — the seeds are expensive, 120 yuan per mu for the hybrid F1, but the melons sell for 1.5-2 yuan per jin if I'm lucky. I put down a lot of chicken manure first, then some compound fertilizer. Need to irrigate three times and watch for fungus. If it works, I can get 2500-3000 kg per mu. If prices crash, I eat the loss. That's farming.

Total input costs will run me about 3,900 yuan this year. That's a lot of money for a 7-mu farm. My son can help if I really get stuck, but I'd rather not ask. I'll hire some labor for wheat and maize harvest — about 16 days total — because I can't do it all myself anymore at 60. The rest we'll handle as a family.

My biggest worry is fertilizer prices. They went up last year and haven't come down. And the water fees keep rising. But I've farmed through worse years. I'll stick with what I know, watch my neighbors, and hope for decent prices.
